prev.title: [SSL] Getting a Free SSL Certificate with Let's Encrypt on Windows 10

detail.body: # Overview Now that we've obtained an SSL certificate, let's apply it. This is typically applied to a web server like Nginx, or a WAS like Tomcat. This chapter explains the process based on Tomcat 9.0.50. # Applying the Certificate to Tomcat Let's apply the certificate to Tomcat. The method differs depending on whether Tomcat Native is installed. > Tomcat Native > Native modules written in C and JAVA are added to improve Tomcat's performance. On Windows, all you need to do is move a single dll file. If Tomcat Native is set up, you can apply the `pem` file directly; otherwise, you need to convert `pem` into a compatible format such as `jks`. # How to Install Tomcat Native The method for installing Tomcat Native differs depending on the OS. SSL can be applied without installing Tomcat Native, so feel free to skip this step if you're not interested. ## Windows 10 Download the Tomcat Native library from [this link](https://tomcat.apache.org/download-native.cgi). Download [Native 1.2.30 Windows Binaries.zip] partway down the page. After extracting it, you'll find `tcnative-1.dll` in the [bin] folder — installation is complete once you move that DLL to `TOMCAT_HOME_HOME/bin`. ## Linux (CentOS 7 or Later) ``` bash yum -y install tomcat-native ``` If you're on CentOS 7, just run the command above. If a command like this isn't available to you, you'll need to compile it yourself directly from [this link](https://tomcat.apache.org/download-native.cgi). ## Linux (Compiling) You compile the source code yourself. This is explained based on CentOS. ``` bash yum install apr-devel openssl-devel ``` Or, if you're on a Debian-based system: ``` bash apt-get install libapr1.0-dev libssl-dev ``` The tools above need to be installed before compiling. Download [Native 1.2.30 Source Release tar.gz] from [this link](https://tomcat.apache.org/download-native.cgi) and extract it. ``` bash tar -zxvf Native 1.2.30 Source Release tar.gz ``` Extract it using the command above; the exact command may differ depending on your OS. ``` bash cd ${extraction_path} ./configure --with-apr=/usr --prefix=${current_path} --with-java-home=${JAVA_HOME} make make install ``` Just run the commands above in sequence. # Applying the SSL Certificate Let's apply the SSL certificate. The method differs depending on whether Tomcat Native is applied. ## Applying a PEM File with Tomcat Native Open the `TOMCAT_HOME/conf/server.xml` file. ``` xml ``` Just edit it as shown above. Set the path to the `crt.pem` file in `SSLCertificateFile`, and the path to the `key.pem` file in `SSLCertificateKeyFile`. ## Converting PEM to JKS and Applying It to a Regular Tomcat Install If, for whatever reason, you can't install Tomcat Native, a regular Tomcat install can't recognize PEM files. So you need to convert it into a format Tomcat supports. In this document, we'll convert it into a `.jks` file and apply that instead. Here's what you'll need: * OpenSSL * keytool (comes bundled with JAVA) You need to install [OpenSSL](https://www.openssl.org/source/) yourself, but keytool is located in `JAVA_HOME/bin`, so if you have JAVA installed, there's no need to install it separately. ``` batch # pem to p12 openssl pkcs12 -export -out {name}.p12 -in {crt}.pem -inkey {key}.pem # p12 to jks keytool -importkeystore -srckeystore {name}.p12 -srcstoretype pkcs12 -destkeystore {name}.jks -deststoretype jks ``` Just run the commands above in order. During the conversion process, you'll be asked for a password to store with the certificate. You'll need to provide this same password to the web server later on, so make sure to remember it. Unlike the 4 `.pem` files, `.jks` is simple and generates just a single file. Once it's generated, open the `TOMCAT_HOME/conf/server.xml` file. ``` xml ``` Enter the `.jks` file you generated in `keystoreFile`, and the password you entered during the conversion process in `keystorePass`. # Verification In this document, the SSL port was set to `443`. Since 443 is the default port for SSL, it will connect automatically without needing to specify the port separately. ![null](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50317129/130097706-8a3cc174-e35d-46db-9f60-caa585a59d98.png) Now start up Tomcat and try accessing your domain. If the certificate information shows up correctly, you've succeeded. For reference, the certificate operates based on the domain. If you access it via `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or an IP address, a certificate error will appear, so keep that in mind. # Summary With this, SSL has been successfully applied. It might look a bit complicated at first, but once you've done it once, there's really nothing too difficult about it. Let's Encrypt is the easiest and fastest way to obtain a DV certificate for free, so make good use of it whenever you need SSL.
